phonemes.desc: Open unrounded vowel [a], the first syllable of the Avestan name.
Long [aː], the stem vowel held and resonant.
Short [h] plus [i], the middle syllable carrying the stress in the restored form.
Long final [aː], the feminine ending that completes the divine name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-NAH-hee-tah' — the stress settles on the penultimate syllable, and the final vowel is drawn out.

kin.label: Etymology

pronunciation.note: Anāhitā is Tier 1 because the restored form preserves distinctive length and the macron-bearing ā, features the ASCII form anahita flattens entirely.

domains.title: The Immaculate Waters
domains.subtitle: Fertility, Healing, and Wisdom
domains.lead: Anāhitā is the great Yazata of the Avestan pantheon, the goddess of the life-giving waters, and one of the most widely worshipped deities of ancient Iran. She is called Aredvi Sura Anāhitā — the moist, strong, undefiled — and her realm runs from the mythical river that surrounds the world to the springs that nourish fields, wombs, and kings.

cards.name: Lady of the Waters
cards.desc: The Avestan Yasht 5 hymns her as the source of all rivers, the force that makes the cosmos fertile and clean.

cards.name: Fertility and Royalty
cards.desc: Kings pray to her for legitimacy, warriors for victory, women for safe childbirth, and farmers for abundant crops.

cards.name: Star of the Waters
cards.desc: She is linked to the planet Venus in later tradition — the bright star that rises from and governs the waters.

cards.name: Golden Splendor
cards.desc: The hymn describes her clothing of gold, her crown, her earrings, and her necklaces — a figure of Iranian royal magnificence.

symbols.name: Running water
symbols.meaning: The river, spring, or canal that is her body and her blessing

symbols.name: Lotus
symbols.meaning: The flower that rises from the water, a later emblem of her purity and fertility

symbols.name: Star (Venus)
symbols.meaning: The celestial body identified with Anāhitā in Sasanian and later Zoroastrian tradition

symbols.name: Golden dress and crown
symbols.meaning: The royal insignia described in Yasht 5, marking her as patron of legitimate kingship

mythology.lead: Anāhitā's mythology flows through the fifth Yašt — the great hymn that names her the mighty river of the world and lists the kings, heroes, and empires that sought her favor — and onward into Achaemenid inscriptions, Sasanian star-lore, and the temples of Armenia. She is a goddess of water who became a goddess of empire, and finally a morning star.

myths.title: The River That Girds the World
myths.text: Aredvi Sura Anāhitā is first a river — the great, the far-famed — rising on Mount Hara and pouring into the sea Vourukaša, whence all the waters of the world are distributed (Yašt 5.3–5). Her hymn is the fifth of the Avestan hymns, recited still in the liturgy of the waters, and it moves between cosmic geography and personal petition: the same goddess who girdles the world with a mythical stream also makes the womb fertile and gives easy childbirth (Yašt 5.2). The hymn's theology is hydrological: to praise Anāhitā is to acknowledge that every canal, spring, and cloud is one circulation. Between these poles the hymn ranges for over a hundred stanzas, and its very length is a theology: no praise of the waters can be too long. The goddess is the water cycle personified — and her immaculate name is an ecological creed, since her worshippers vow to keep her element clean.

myths.title: The Beaver Mantle and the Chariot of Storms
myths.text: Yašt 5 describes her coming to sacrifice on a chariot drawn by four horses — wind, rain, cloud, and sleet (5.16) — splendid in gold, bright and tall, with white arms (5.123–125). Most striking is her mantle: thirty beaver skins, taken from four-year-old beavers, worn so that the seed and evil eye of the daevas cannot touch her body (5.126–129). Modern readers often misread the passage as luxury; the hymn's logic is purity, not wealth — every element of her dress is armor against defilement, and the worship she accepts begins with purification rites (yaozdāθra) performed before sacrifice. The detail fascinated antiquity: classical writers echo these lines when they describe the dress of Persian noblewomen at her festivals. Anāhitā's golden splendor is a visual theology of integrity — beauty as the radiance of what cannot be stained.

myths.title: The Empire Adopts a Goddess
myths.text: Anāhitā crosses from scripture into state religion under Artaxerxes II (r. 404–359 BCE), whose inscriptions invoke her between Ahura Mazdā and Mithra: may Auramazdā, Anāhitā, and Mithra protect me (A²Sa, A²Sd). Berossus, quoted by Clement of Alexandria, reports that the king raised statues of Anaitis in Babylon, Susa, Ecbatana, Persepolis, Bactra, Damascus, and Sardis (Protrepticus 5.65); whether or not every temple stood, the claim shows what the cult meant — a single goddess binding the empire's provinces into one sacred geography. Strabo still describes her great sanctuary in Media centuries later (Geography 11.8.4). Herodotus, a century earlier, already lists the Persian gods under interpretive Greek names — the first step in a long career of identification (Histories 1.131–132). Anāhitā's temples were the empire made visible in stone — each a node of loyalty as much as of piety.

myths.title: Anahid, Morning Star of the Lake
myths.text: In Sasanian theology the goddess became a star. The Bundahišn names Anāhīd the brightest and chief of the fixed stars and mistress of the waters, and the royal tradition honored her flame, Ādur-Anāhīd, among the great sanctuary fires (Bundahišn 5, 17). The eighth month of the Zoroastrian year, Ābān, 'Waters', was dedicated to her element, with its feast Ābānagān in mid-autumn; on the day-dedication hymns to the waters rose in every fire temple of the realm, and the planet Venus — brightest of the wandering lights — was read as her presence. The transformation is the reverse of a demotion: Her fire was tended by a hereditary priesthood whose endowments and privileges the Pahlavi law books record in royal detail. by becoming the morning star, Anāhitā ceased to belong to any one sanctuary and acquired the whole sky as her temple.

myths.title: The Temple of Erez and the Golden Cauldron
myths.text: Anāhitā's farthest great cult was Armenian. Agathangelos' History of the Armenians (5th century) describes her temple at Erez, stocked with the gold and silver of generations — a great cauldron among the treasures — which Gregory the Illuminator, after converting King Trdat, dismantled and melted down. Faustus of Byzantium adds that her feast drew the noblest families, who dedicated horses and harness to her (History of Armenia 5). The episode is told from the victors' side, and its very hostility is testimony: to erase Anāhitā's cult cost an empire's effort. Traces of her cult lingered in folk custom for centuries; village water rites kept her memory after her statues were gone. The goddess Christianity could not absorb, it commemorated by the labor of destroying her — the surest measure of how deeply Armenia had loved her.

lore.syncretism: Anāhitā absorbed and was absorbed by neighboring goddesses. In Armenia she was identified with the indigenous goddess Nana or Nanē, and with the Greek Artemis and Tyche. The Seleucid and Parthian periods saw her portrayed in Hellenistic dress with a mural crown, tympanum, and lions — the visual vocabulary of the Syrian goddess Atargatis. Some scholars compare her functions to those of the Mesopotamian Ishtar/Inanna and the Indic Sarasvatī, though these are typological parallels, not direct borrowings. She is best understood as an Iranian development of the ancient Near Eastern goddess of water, fertility, and sovereignty.
lore.culturalLegacy: Anāhitā's name lived on in Iranian languages as Anāhīd, a popular female name and a poetic word for the planet Venus. The pre-Islamic Iranian new year, Nawrōz, preserved water-rituals that honored her. In modern Zoroastrian practice, the veneration of water and the divine feminine continues, and Anāhitā remains one of the best-known Yazatas outside the tradition. Her temples at Kangāvar and Bīšāpūr are among the most impressive surviving monuments of Sasanian religion. Restoring Anāhitā recovers the long vowels and stress that distinguish the Avestan goddess from the flattened modern name.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Anāhitā is the water that knows no stain. In a religious world dominated by fire and light, she represents the sacred power of moisture, fertility, and the female divine. Her name means undefiled, and her cult asks human beings to keep the waters clean — an ecological commandment older than any modern environmentalism.

She is also a royal goddess, the patron of legitimate rule, and her hymn is a catalogue of the great who sought her favor. To meditate on Anāhitā is to meditate on the waters that make civilization possible: the river, the spring, the canal, the womb. She asks not for war but for purity, not for conquest but for the careful tending of life.

lore.archaeology: Major temples dedicated to Anāhitā have been identified at Kangāvar (often identified with the temple of Artemis/Anāhitā mentioned by Isidore of Charax), Bīšāpūr, and Takht-e Soleymān. Sasanian and Kushano-Sasanian coinage depicts her with mural crown, lotus, and lions. Achaemenid inscriptions from Susa and Hamadan name her alongside Ahura Mazdā and Mithra, confirming her place in the official cult of the empire.
